title: Relational operators: joins, aggregation and planning
summary: How a database runs SQL: plan trees of pull-based operators, nested loop, merge and hash joins, hash vs sorted aggregation, memory spills, and how a cost-based planner searches join orders using row estimates.
outcomes: Read an EXPLAIN plan tree and explain startup cost, total cost, rows and loops
Trace nested loop, merge and hash joins on small inputs and compare their work
Explain why the best join flips with row counts and when hash joins and aggregates spill
Choose between HashAggregate and GroupAggregate and combine partial aggregate states
Explain dynamic programming join search, GEQO, and why row misestimates cause slow plans

lessons.title: A query plan is a tree of operators that pull rows

blocks.md:
SQL says *what* rows you want, not *how* to find them. The same query can be answered by reading a whole table, by walking a B-tree index (from the previous course), or by joining tables in different orders with different algorithms. Every choice returns the same rows, but run times can differ by orders of magnitude.

The **planner** (also called the optimizer) picks one way to run the query. The **executor** then runs it. This course is about the pieces the executor runs, called **relational operators**, and how the planner chooses between them. We use PostgreSQL as the running example because its docs and source explain every step.

A plan is a tree of **plan nodes**. The leaves are **scan nodes** that return raw rows from a table: a sequential scan reads every page, an index scan walks an index, a bitmap scan collects row locations from an index and then reads the pages in physical order.

Above the scans sit nodes for joins, sorting and aggregation. Most nodes can also do **selection** (drop rows that fail a condition, shown as `Filter:` in EXPLAIN) and **projection** (compute only the output columns needed).

blocks.title: One plan tree, pulled from the top

scenes.caption: The plan for a two-table join with ORDER BY, from the PostgreSQL EXPLAIN docs. Leaves read tables, the middle joins, the top sorts. Rows flow up the arrows.
The client asks the top node for a row. Sort cannot answer yet: it must see every input row before it knows which one is first, so it asks the Hash Join below it.
Hash Join first drains its inner child. The bitmap scans find the 100 rows of tenk1 with unique1 < 100, and Hash loads them into an in-memory hash table.
Now Hash Join pulls tenk2 one row at a time from the Seq Scan and looks each one up in the hash table. 10000 rows are scanned, 100 match and go up.
Only after the join reports it is done can Sort sort its 100 rows and hand the first one to the client. Sort is a blocking node; the scans and the probe were pipelined.

blocks.md:
PostgreSQL's docs call the executor a **demand-pull pipeline**: each time a node is called it must deliver one more row or report that it is done. A parent pulls from its children only when it needs a row.

This gives two kinds of node. **Pipelined** nodes such as a scan with a filter pass each row up as soon as they have it. **Blocking** nodes such as Sort, or the Hash that builds a hash table, must consume their whole input before producing anything.

blocks.code:
EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM tenk1 ORDER BY unique1;

 Sort  (cost=1109.39..1134.39 rows=10000 width=244)
   Sort Key: unique1
   ->  Seq Scan on tenk1  (cost=0.00..445.00 rows=10000 width=244)
blocks.caption: From the PostgreSQL docs (Using EXPLAIN). Indentation shows the tree: Seq Scan is the child of Sort.

blocks.md:
Each EXPLAIN line shows four estimates: **startup cost** (work before the first row can come out), **total cost** (work to return all rows), **rows** (rows this node *emits*, not rows it reads) and **width** (average bytes per row).

Costs are in arbitrary units where one sequential page read costs `seq_page_cost` = 1.0 by default. A parent's cost includes all of its children. Look at the Sort above: its startup cost 1109.39 is almost its total 1134.39, because nearly all its work happens before the first row.

blocks.caption: The docs' tenk1 table has 345 pages and 10000 rows. Defaults: seq_page_cost 1.0, cpu_tuple_cost 0.01.

blocks.prompt: Now run `EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM tenk1 WHERE unique1 < 7000`. About 7000 of 10000 rows pass. Does the estimated cost of the Seq Scan go up, go down, or stay at 445?
blocks.reveal: It goes **up**, to 470. The scan still has to read all 345 pages and look at all 10000 rows; it just emits fewer (rows=7000). Checking the condition costs one `cpu_operator_cost` (0.0025) per row, so 10000 x 0.0025 = 25 is added. A filter on a sequential scan never saves reading; only an index can skip pages.

scenes.caption: SELECT * FROM tenk1: 345 sequential page reads at seq_page_cost 1.0 plus 10000 rows at cpu_tuple_cost 0.01. Total 445, matching EXPLAIN.
Add WHERE unique1 < 7000: every row is still read, and each one now costs one operator call (cpu_operator_cost 0.0025). The total rises by 25 to 470 even though fewer rows come out.

blocks.md: A plan is a tree of operators. Leaves scan, inner nodes join, sort and aggregate, and rows are pulled upward one at a time. The `rows` number is what a node emits, and a node's cost includes everything below it.
Cost units are not milliseconds. They are relative estimates the planner uses to compare plans. To see real time, use EXPLAIN ANALYZE, which actually runs the query.

blocks.question: A plan shows `Sort (cost=1109.39..1134.39 rows=10000)` above a Seq Scan costing 445. Why is the Sort's startup cost so close to its total cost?
options: Sorting 10000 rows is cheap, so both numbers are small
Sort must read and sort all of its input before it can return the first row
The startup cost counts only the time to send rows to the client
The planner charges the Seq Scan twice
blocks.explain: Sort is a blocking node. Its first output row is the smallest key, which it cannot know until it has seen every input row. So almost all the work (the child scan plus the sort) lands in the startup cost, and returning the rows afterwards adds only 25 units.

blocks.question: An Index Scan below a LIMIT 2 shows `cost=0.29..70.27 rows=10`. The planner assumes rows are spread evenly over the scan. About what total cost does it give the Limit node?
options: 70.27, the child's full cost
0.29, only the startup cost
About 14.3
About 7.0, one tenth of the child
blocks.explain: The Limit stops after 2 of the expected 10 rows, so it pays the startup cost plus 2/10 of the rest: 0.29 + (70.27 - 0.29) x 0.2 = 14.29. The docs show this exact plan with Limit cost 0.29..14.28. This is why LIMIT can change which plan wins: plans with a low startup cost become attractive.

lessons.title: Three ways to join two tables

blocks.md:
All PostgreSQL joins combine exactly two inputs; bigger joins are trees of two-input joins. The docs list three algorithms: **nested loop**, **merge join** and **hash join**. We will run all three on the same tiny inputs.

R has join keys 7, 2, 9, 5 (4 rows). S has keys 5, 9, 1, 7, 5, 3 (6 rows). The correct answer is 4 rows: 7 with 7, 9 with 9, and 5 with each of the two 5s in S.

**Nested loop**: for each row of the *outer* input, scan the whole *inner* input and keep the pairs that satisfy the join condition. It is the simplest algorithm and the only one that works for any condition, such as `t1.hundred < t2.hundred`. Its cost is roughly outer rows times the cost of one inner scan.

blocks.title: Nested loop: every outer row against every inner row

scenes.caption: Outer row 7 is compared with all 6 inner rows. One match, at the fourth inner row. 6 comparisons so far.
Outer row 2: all 6 inner rows are scanned again and none match. The work is wasted but still paid. 12 comparisons.
Outer row 9 matches the second inner row. 18 comparisons.
Outer row 5 matches two inner rows. Done: 4 x 6 = 24 comparisons to find 4 result rows.

blocks.md: Nested loop becomes good when the inner scan is an **index scan**. The executor plugs the current outer row's key into the inner index lookup (`Index Cond: (unique2 = t1.unique2)` in EXPLAIN), so each loop costs one B-tree descent instead of a full scan. With few outer rows this is often the cheapest plan of all.

**Merge join**: sort both inputs on the join key, then walk them together with one pointer each, always advancing the pointer at the smaller key. Each input is scanned once. The sort can be an explicit Sort node, or free if an index already returns rows in key order. If the outer side has duplicate keys, the executor *marks* the first matching inner row and *restores* to it for the next outer row.

blocks.title: Merge join: two sorted inputs, two pointers

scenes.caption: Both inputs are sorted. Compare 2 with 1: the inner key is smaller, so 1 cannot match anything later in R. Advance the inner pointer.
Compare 2 with 3: now the outer key is smaller, so 2 has no partner anywhere in S. Advance the outer pointer.
Compare 5 with 3: inner is smaller. Advance the inner pointer.
5 equals 5: emit a joined row. The executor marks this inner position, because the next outer row might also be 5 and need to rescan from here.
The next inner row is also 5: emit a second row. Duplicates on the inner side are simply walked over.
Inner 7 ended the run of 5s. Advance outer to 7. It is not 5, so no restore to the mark is needed. 7 equals 7: emit.
Advance both to 9: emit. Either input is now exhausted, so the join ends. Each input was walked once: 4 outer steps and 6 inner steps.

blocks.md: **Hash join**: first read the inner input and load it into an in-memory hash table keyed on the join columns (the **build** phase). Then stream the outer input and look up each row's key in the table (the **probe** phase). Both inputs are read once, and neither needs to be sorted. The figure uses key mod 4 as a toy hash; PostgreSQL uses a real hash function and many more buckets.

blocks.title: Hash join: build a table on R, probe it with S

scenes.caption: Build phase starts. Simplified hash function: bucket = key mod 4. The hash table has 4 empty buckets.
Insert build rows 7 (7 mod 4 = 3) and 2 (bucket 2). Each insert is one hash plus one append.
Insert 9 and 5: both land in bucket 1, a collision. The build side is done after 4 inserts, one pass over R.
Probe phase: stream S. Row 5 hashes to bucket 1, which holds 9 and 5. Two key checks, one match, emitted at once.
Row 9 also goes to bucket 1: two checks, one match. Running total: 4 checks.
Row 1 goes to bucket 1 too. Two checks, no match. Collisions cost extra checks but never wrong answers, because keys are compared exactly.
Row 7 goes to bucket 3, holding only 7: one check, one match. Total 7 checks.
The second 5 goes to bucket 1: two checks, one match. Total 9 checks.
Row 3 goes to bucket 3: one check, no match. Done: 10 key checks plus 4 inserts, versus 24 comparisons for the nested loop. Same 4 result rows.

blocks.md: Nested loop: cost about outer x inner-scan, works for any condition, great with an inner index and few outer rows. Merge join: one pass over each sorted input, needs sorted inputs and an equality key. Hash join: one pass over each input, needs an equality key and memory for the build side.
In EXPLAIN, the first child of a join is the outer input and the second is the inner. For a hash join the inner child is wrapped in a `Hash` node: that is the side being built into the table.

blocks.question: A query joins on `t1.hundred < t2.hundred` (an inequality). Which join algorithm can PostgreSQL use for this condition?
options: Hash join, because it is the fastest
Merge join, because both sides can be sorted
Nested loop, checking the condition for each pair
None; inequality joins are not supported
blocks.explain: Hash join needs equal keys to land in the same bucket, and PostgreSQL's merge join works on equality clauses of the form outerKey = innerKey. Only nested loop can evaluate an arbitrary condition, which EXPLAIN shows as a `Join Filter` on the Nested Loop node (this exact query is an example in the docs).

blocks.question: The outer side of a join yields 10 rows after a filter. The inner table has 10000 rows and a B-tree index on the join key. Which plan is most likely cheapest?
options: Nested loop with an index scan on the inner side
Hash join, building on the 10000-row table
Merge join after sorting both sides
Nested loop with a sequential scan of the inner side
blocks.explain: Ten index lookups touch only a few pages each, while a hash join must read all 10000 inner rows once. The PostgreSQL docs show exactly this case (unique1 < 10) choosing Nested Loop with an inner Index Scan. A nested loop with a sequential inner scan would read the 10000-row table 10 times.

lessons.title: When each join wins: row counts, probes and memory

blocks.md: The planner does not pick a join algorithm by rule of thumb. It estimates a cost for every applicable algorithm and keeps the cheapest. The PostgreSQL docs show how sharply the winner changes with the number of outer rows, using the same two 10000-row tables.

blocks.code:
WHERE t1.unique1 < 10 AND t1.unique2 = t2.unique2
 Nested Loop  (cost=4.65..118.50 rows=10 width=488)
   ->  Bitmap Heap Scan on tenk1 t1  (cost=4.36..39.38 rows=10 width=244)
   ->  Index Scan using tenk2_unique2 on tenk2 t2  (cost=0.29..7.90 rows=1 width=244)

WHERE t1.unique1 < 100 AND t1.unique2 = t2.unique2
 Hash Join  (cost=226.23..709.73 rows=100 width=488)
   ->  Seq Scan on tenk2 t2  (cost=0.00..445.00 rows=10000 width=244)
   ->  Hash  (cost=224.98..224.98 rows=100 width=244)
blocks.caption: Abridged from the PostgreSQL docs. Same tables, ten times more outer rows, different algorithm.

blocks.md:
The docs explain the first total: the outer scan (39.38) plus one inner index scan per outer row (10 x 7.90 = 79.0), plus a little CPU for the join itself. That is 118.38 before the small join CPU, against the reported 118.50.

With 100 outer rows, 100 probes would cost about 790, more than simply reading tenk2 once (445) and probing a hash table built from the 100 rows.

blocks.title: Inner-side cost: index nested loop vs hash join

params.name: p
params.label: cost of one inner index probe

curves.label: hash join: one scan of tenk2

scenes.caption: Simplified model using the docs' numbers: each inner index probe costs 7.90, while a hash join reads tenk2 once for 445. The lines cross near 56 outer rows. Real costing also adds CPU per row and the hash build.
At 10 outer rows the loop costs 79, far below 445: the docs' plan for unique1 < 10 is a Nested Loop. At 100 rows it would cost 790, and the docs' plan for unique1 < 100 is a Hash Join.
If probes were cheaper (say 3.0, more pages cached), the crossover moves out to about 148 rows. The best algorithm depends on both the row estimate and the per-probe cost.

blocks.prompt: The planner estimated 10 outer rows and chose the nested loop. At run time the filter actually passes 5000 rows. Using the 7.90 per probe from the docs, roughly how does the loop's inner cost compare with the hash join's one scan of 445?
blocks.reveal: 5000 x 7.90 = 39,500 units, about 89 times the 445 a single scan of tenk2 would cost. The plan was optimal *for the estimate* and badly wrong for reality. This is why wrong row estimates, not wrong algorithms, are the usual cause of slow plans, and why the last lesson is about estimates.

blocks.md:
Hash join has its own risk: memory. The hash table may use up to `work_mem` x `hash_mem_multiplier`, which is 4 MB x 2.0 = 8 MB with PostgreSQL's defaults. If the build side is bigger, the join splits both inputs into **batches** by hash value, following the hybrid hash join of Zeller and Gray (1990).

Batch 0 is joined in memory while the others are written to temporary files and joined later, one batch at a time. Matching keys always share a batch because they have the same hash. The number of batches is a power of two, and the executor doubles it if a batch still turns out too big.

blocks.title: Hash join in two batches when memory runs out

scenes.caption: Suppose R does not fit in memory, so the join uses nbatch = 2. Each key gets a batch number from hash bits above the bucket bits. With our toy hash that is floor(key / 4) mod 2: R keys 2 and 9 fall in batch 0, and 7 and 5 in batch 1.
Build: batch 0 rows (2, 9) go into the in-memory hash table. Batch 1 rows (7, 5) are written to a temporary file for later. Memory now holds only half of R.
Probe: S rows are hashed the same way. Batch 0 rows (9, 1, 3) probe the table now; 9 finds its match. Batch 1 rows (5, 7, 5) are written to their own temp file instead.

Batch 1: reload R's 7 and 5 from disk into a fresh hash table, then read S's 5, 7, 5 back and probe. Three more matches. Total: the same 4 rows, at the price of writing and rereading part of both inputs.

blocks.md: `work_mem` is a limit per sort or hash operation, not per query. A plan with three hash joins and a sort can use several multiples of it, and many sessions can do so at once. Raising it globally to fix one query can exhaust memory.

EXPLAIN ANALYZE prints `Buckets: 1024  Batches: 1  Memory Usage: 35kB` on a Hash node. `Batches` above 1 means the build side spilled to disk. Also watch for a Memoize node in nested loops: it caches inner results for repeated parameter values.

blocks.question: EXPLAIN ANALYZE shows a Hash node with `Batches: 16`. What does that tell you?
options: The hash table had 16 buckets
The build side did not fit in hash memory, so both inputs were split and partly written to temp files
The join ran on 16 parallel workers
The planner tried 16 join orders
blocks.explain: Batches count partitions of the hash join. More than one means the inner input exceeded work_mem x hash_mem_multiplier, so rows of later batches were written to and reread from disk. Remedies: give the operation more memory, build on a smaller input, or filter rows earlier.

blocks.question: Which input should a hash join normally build its hash table on?
options: The larger input, so probing is cheaper
Whichever comes first in the FROM clause
The input that is already sorted
The smaller input, so the table fits in memory
blocks.explain: Build cost and memory grow with the build side, while each probe is a constant-time lookup either way. Building on the smaller input keeps the table in memory and avoids batching. In the docs' plan the Hash node sits over the 100-row tenk1 scan, not the 10000-row tenk2.

lessons.title: Aggregation and sorting: running state, hash tables and spills

blocks.md: An aggregate such as `count`, `sum` or `avg` folds many rows into one value. PostgreSQL's executor does it with a **transition state**: start from an initial value, update it with a *transition function* for each input row, and at the end apply an optional *final function*.

blocks.caption: For avg the state is the pair (count, sum), and the final function divides sum by count.

blocks.md:
With `GROUP BY` there is one state per group, and the executor needs to find the right state for each row. PostgreSQL has two main strategies, named in EXPLAIN:

- **HashAggregate**: keep a hash table from group key to state. Any input order works; groups come out only at the end.
- **GroupAggregate**: require input sorted by the group key, keep a single state, and emit a group whenever the key changes.

A query with aggregates but no GROUP BY uses a plain `Aggregate` node with a single state. Our example: `SELECT model, avg(latency_ms) FROM runs GROUP BY model` over six rows.

blocks.title: HashAggregate: one state per group in a hash table

scenes.caption: Row (a, 30): group a is new, so a state is created with count 1 and sum 30. The state is shown as count/sum.
Row (b, 10): new group b. The table now holds two states.
Row (a, 50): the hash lookup finds group a and the transition function updates it to 2/80. Nothing is emitted yet.
Row (c, 20): third group. Memory grows with the number of distinct groups, not the number of rows.
Row (b, 30): b becomes 2/40.
Row (a, 40): a becomes 3/120. The input is done, so only now can any group be finished.
Final function: avg = sum / count, giving a 40, b 20, c 20. A HashAggregate returns groups in hash table order, so they are not sorted.

blocks.title: GroupAggregate: sorted input, one state at a time

scenes.caption: The same rows, sorted by model. Only one state is kept: after the three a rows it is 3/120.
The first b row changes the key, so group a is complete: emit a = 120/3 = 40 and reset the state. Output starts streaming before the input ends.
c changes the key again: emit b = 40/2 = 20. End of input: emit c = 20. Same answer as the hash version, in sorted order, using one state of memory.

blocks.md: The tradeoff mirrors hash join versus merge join. HashAggregate needs no sort, but its memory grows with the number of distinct groups. GroupAggregate needs sorted input, from a Sort node or an index in key order, but uses almost no memory, streams results, and its output is already ordered for a matching ORDER BY.

If the hash table outgrows its memory limit (work_mem x hash_mem_multiplier), PostgreSQL's HashAggregate enters **spill mode**: rows for groups already in the table keep updating their states, while rows that would create a new group are written to disk in hash partitions. Each partition is aggregated later; one that is still too big is spilled again recursively.

**Sort** has the same memory question. EXPLAIN ANALYZE prints the method: `quicksort` when everything fit in memory, `external sort` or `external merge` when it had to use temp files, or `top-N heapsort` when a LIMIT means only the first N rows are needed. An **Incremental Sort** can reuse an order that a child already provides on a prefix of the keys, and so can return rows before all input is sorted.

blocks.prompt: Two queries over the same 100 million rows: `GROUP BY country` (about 200 distinct values) and `GROUP BY user_id` (about 50 million distinct values). Which one is more likely to make a HashAggregate spill?
blocks.reveal: `GROUP BY user_id`. HashAggregate memory is roughly the number of groups times the state size, not the number of input rows. 200 states fit easily; 50 million states probably do not fit in a few MB, so the planner may prefer sorting (or an index on user_id) and a GroupAggregate, or the hash aggregate will spill partitions to disk.

blocks.md: Aggregation keeps a small state per group. Hashing finds the state with a table (memory grows with groups); sorting brings each group together so one state suffices (needs ordered input). Sort and hash nodes both spill to disk when they exceed their memory limit.
A GROUP BY result from a HashAggregate has no defined order. If you need sorted output, write ORDER BY; do not rely on the order you happened to see.

blocks.question: For parallel aggregation, two workers compute partial results for group a. Worker 1 saw 30; worker 2 saw 50 and 40. What should the final step combine to get avg = 40?
options: The two averages, 30 and 45, averaged to 37.5
The two states (1, 30) and (2, 90), added to (3, 120), then 120 / 3
Only the larger worker's average, 45
The two averages weighted equally, then rounded
blocks.explain: Averaging averages gives 37.5, which is wrong. The correct merge combines transition states: counts add and sums add, then the final function divides once. PostgreSQL supports this with combine functions for partial aggregation; the merge works on states, not on finished results.

blocks.question: A query has `GROUP BY model ORDER BY model` and there is a B-tree index on model. Which plan shape avoids both a hash table and an explicit Sort?
options: Seq Scan, then HashAggregate, then Sort
Seq Scan, then Sort, then HashAggregate
Bitmap Heap Scan, then HashAggregate
Index Scan in model order, then GroupAggregate
blocks.explain: An index scan returns rows already ordered by model, which is exactly what GroupAggregate needs, and its output stays in model order so the ORDER BY is free. Whether this beats a seq scan plus HashAggregate depends on the cost of random index access versus sequential reading, which the planner estimates.

lessons.title: How the planner chooses: join order search and row estimates

blocks.md:
With three tables a, b, c and conditions a.id = b.id and b.ref = c.id, the planner can join (a, b) then c, or (b, c) then a. Joining a with c first is legal but has no join condition, so it forms the full Cartesian product. All orders give the same result; their costs can differ enormously.

The PostgreSQL docs say the number of orders grows exponentially, and that beyond about ten tables exhaustive search is no longer practical.

blocks.title: How many ways to join n tables?

scenes.caption: Left-deep plans join one new table at a time, so each is an ordering of the n tables: n! of them. 4 tables give 24, 12 tables give about 479 million.
Allowing bushy trees, where both inputs of a join can be joins, gives (2n-2)!/(n-1)! ordered trees: 120 for 4 tables and about 2.8e13 for 12. Listing them one by one is hopeless.

Dynamic programming instead stores the cheapest plan for each subset of tables and builds bigger subsets from smaller ones. There are only 2^n - 1 subsets: 4095 for 12 tables, though the work per level still grows quickly.

blocks.md:
PostgreSQL's standard search uses **dynamic programming**, the classic cost-based approach that dates back to IBM's System R. For each set of tables it keeps the best ways found to produce that set, then builds the next level from them. It considers left-deep, right-deep and bushy shapes, and tries every join algorithm for each pair.

It keeps more than one path per set: a path survives if it is cheaper in total cost, cheaper in startup cost, emits fewer rows, or has a more useful **sort order**. A pricier path that is already sorted can win later by enabling a merge join or a free ORDER BY.

blocks.title: Join search level by level (PostgreSQL optimizer README)

scenes.caption: Query: tab1.col = tab2.col AND tab2.col = tab3.col AND tab3.col = tab4.col. Level 1: the cheapest scan path for each table.

Level 2: join pairs that share a join clause: {1 2}, {2 3}, {3 4}. Simplified as in the README: real PostgreSQL also derives tab1.col = tab3.col from the equalities, so {1 3} would not really be a Cartesian product.
Level 3: {1 2 3} and {2 3 4}. Each is built from the stored best plans of smaller sets, with every join algorithm tried. All ways of making the same set compete, and only the useful paths survive.
Level 4: the final set can come from {1 2 3} plus 4, 1 plus {2 3 4}, or the bushy {1 2} joined with {3 4} (dashed). The cheapest total becomes the plan.

blocks.md:
Beyond a threshold PostgreSQL switches to the **Genetic Query Optimizer** (GEQO). It treats join order like a traveling salesman problem: a plan is encoded as a string such as `4-1-3-2` (join 4 and 1, then 3, then 2), and a genetic algorithm evolves good strings. It plans faster but may miss the best plan.

Defaults: `geqo_threshold` = 12 FROM items. `from_collapse_limit` and `join_collapse_limit` are 8, so larger subqueries and explicit JOIN lists are not flattened into a single search.

Every cost depends on **row estimates**. They come from statistics that ANALYZE gathers from a random sample. In the docs' equality join example both columns are unique and have no common-value list, so the selectivity is 1 divided by the larger table's row count, adjusted for nulls. For non-unique columns the planner divides by the larger number of distinct values instead.

blocks.caption: The docs' example: 50 outer rows (from unique1 < 50) joined with the 10000-row tenk2.

blocks.md: Errors in these estimates multiply up the tree. Leis et al. (VLDB 2015) measured this on real data with 113 multi-join queries. The main cause is the **independence assumption**: estimators multiply selectivities as if predicates were unrelated, while real columns are correlated.

blocks.title: Share of join estimates off by 10x or more (Leis et al.)

scenes.caption: PostgreSQL's estimates on the Join Order Benchmark (real IMDB data): 16% are off by at least 10x with one join, 32% with two and 52% with three. Errors compound up the tree.
DBMS A, the best estimator in the study, does only somewhat better: 15%, 25% and 36%. The paper finds all systems tend to underestimate multi-join results.

blocks.md: The same study found that most of PostgreSQL's timeouts came from a nested-loop join without an index, chosen because a tiny row estimate made it look cheapest. When the real input was large, its rows x rows work exploded. A cost-only choice ignores how risky a plan is if the estimate is wrong.

So the practical loop is: run `EXPLAIN ANALYZE`, and compare each node's estimated `rows` with its actual rows. A node executed many times shows `loops`; its actual time and rows are averages per loop, so multiply by loops. The first node where estimate and reality diverge by orders of magnitude is usually the root cause. Fixes include running ANALYZE, extended statistics for correlated columns (CREATE STATISTICS), an index on the join key, or rewriting the query.

blocks.code:
->  Index Scan using tenk2_unique2 on tenk2 t2
      (cost=0.29..7.90 rows=1 width=244)
      (actual time=0.003..0.003 rows=1.00 loops=10)
      Index Cond: (unique2 = t1.unique2)
blocks.caption: The inner side of the docs' nested loop under EXPLAIN ANALYZE: 10 loops, one row each.

blocks.md: The planner is only as good as its row estimates. It searches join orders exhaustively by dynamic programming up to a limit, then genetically; but a 100x row misestimate can turn the cheapest-looking plan into the slowest. Read EXPLAIN ANALYZE estimates against actuals first.

blocks.question: In the snippet above, the inner Index Scan shows `actual time=0.003..0.003 rows=1.00 loops=10`. About how much total time was spent in that node?
options: 0.3 ms
It cannot be known from this line
blocks.explain: Actual time and rows are averages per loop. Multiply by loops: 0.003 ms x 10 = 0.030 ms, the figure the docs give. Forgetting loops is a common way to misread where time goes in nested loops.

blocks.question: A plan estimates `rows=1` for a nested loop's outer input, but EXPLAIN ANALYZE shows 200,000 actual rows and the query is slow. What is the best first fix?
options: Set enable_nestloop = off for the whole server
Raise work_mem so the nested loop fits in memory
Fix the estimate: run ANALYZE, add extended statistics for correlated columns, or add an index
Raise geqo_threshold so more join orders are searched
blocks.explain: The nested loop was chosen because of the 1-row estimate; the algorithm is a symptom. Correcting statistics lets the planner cost the alternatives honestly. Disabling nested loops globally hurts the many queries where an index nested loop is best, and work_mem and GEQO do not affect this estimate.

blocks.question: A query joins 14 tables listed in FROM with default settings. How does PostgreSQL search for a join order?
options: With the Genetic Query Optimizer, since 14 is at least geqo_threshold (12)
Exhaustive dynamic programming over all 14 tables
It joins them in the order written
It refuses to plan queries over 12 tables
blocks.explain: GEQO is used for queries with at least geqo_threshold FROM items, 12 by default. It finds a reasonable order quickly but not necessarily the best. Exhaustive search would cost too much planning time at this size.
